output.headline: Government invests in early intervention and specialist bases for Send reform
output.bodyHtml:
The government is already investing in early intervention and specialist bases, deliberately taking a slow, phased approach to overhauling special education in England, according to the author of new analysis – which also says that Labour’s flagship changes are at risk of unravelling because parents are rushing to secure support for their children before the system changes, with councils projecting that nearly one in 10 pupils will have an education, health and care plan (EHCP) by 2029.

The Institute for Government (IfG) thinktank says the government’s plans to largely replace education, health and care plans (EHCPs) in England with more widespread support in mainstream schools may be too optimistic and take longer to complete than its 2030 timeline.

The thinktank’s report calls on the government to review the timetable for the changes. And it suggests that if ministers do not act they “risk basing both their reforms and spending plans on assumptions that the system cannot deliver”.

The news will be seen as a sign that the government’s ambitious plans to overhaul the special education system did not reckon with the scale of worry among parents, many of whom appear to have acted to ensure support and avoid uncertainty in the future.

Related: Pupils with Send plans in England likely to double to one in 10 in rush for support

The Guardian recently reported that councils and schools have reported a surge in applications for EHCPs, with one school describing the level as “unreal” compared with previous years. Several councils are now projecting that at the current rates of increase, nearly one in 10 pupils will have an EHCP by 2029.

Amber Dellar, the author of the IfG report out this week, said the long rollout of the changes created a “moral hazard” that encouraged parents to apply for EHCPs now rather than wait for the new system.

“There’s a ‘use it before you lose it’ dynamic, as schools and parents have an incentive to secure EHCPs before they are phased out, because there’s a lot of uncertainty about what these new specialist packages of support will contain and who will be eligible for them,” she said.

Dellar said the government’s plans added new resources in order to reduce the need for families to seek EHCPs, the individualised packages of support agreed between parents and local authorities that can be enforced by specialist tribunals.

But Dellar said budgets for the additional resources for special educational needs and disabilities (Send) would be eroded if demands for EHCPs shot above the government’s own forecasts, with councils saying they have to keep issuing EHCPs until the existing legislation is repealed.

She said: “The government has a lot riding on the reforms taking effect before they fully kick in – its spending plans for the parliament have some assumptions about savings baked in that are based in particular on them being able to slow the growth or the trajectory of numbers of pupils with EHCPs.

“It has a lot politically riding on it as well, and of course in terms of the wellbeing of the children and families involved.”

A Department for Education (DfE) spokesperson said: “The figures in this report are speculative and there is no evidence that proposed reforms are driving additional EHCP demand.

“We inherited a Send system with record numbers of EHCPs and families waiting months for support. We are already investing to change that, backing schools to improve inclusion, widening access to specialists and rolling out training for every teacher to better support children before needs escalate.

“It is vital that we take the time needed to get this right, but we are completely committed to the implementation timelines set out in the schools white paper and will announce next steps soon.”

The changes announced in February under Keir Starmer’s administration promised to overhaul a system that parents have denounced for forcing them to seek EHCPs to secure specialist support or a place in a special school.

Many parents said the EHCP application process – introduced by the Conservatives in 2014 – required lengthy waits for NHS assessments for conditions such as ADHD or autism, or great expense for those who could afford private assessments. Families then face bureaucratic delays from schools and local authorities, or legal appeals to a specialist Send tribunal to override councils’ objections.

Mark Franks, the director of welfare at the Nuffield Foundation, which funded the report, said: “While there is broad agreement that the current system is under strain, uncertainty and concern remain about whether future levels of investment and the nature of reform will be sufficient to provide high-quality support for all children and young people.”

The IfG said the additional costs of Send provision could erode the extra funding being offered for state schools in England, saying it could absorb “around two-thirds of the generous schools funding uplift over this parliament”.

The package of changes would see mainstream schools given greater support for pupils with special needs, including the creation of specialist bases, allowing pupils to attend local schools and reduce pressure on special schools.

The DfE also wants individual support plans to replace many EHCPs, which would be retained for children with the most profound needs.

The IfG said: “It is not clear exactly how the reforms will slow the growth in EHCPs before the new system is fully in place.”

Related: ‘Powerful example’: minister looks to Essex school for blueprint to transform Send provision

Dellar said: “The government is making investments now, in early intervention and in specialist bases. But the whole way the government is approaching these Send reforms is deliberately to take a slow, phased approach – largely because it knows that those investments are going to take a while to have an effect.

“Its investments in early assessment are going to take a little time to bear fruit. It has not yet properly set out exactly what preventative support it wants schools to put in place. So until schools have that, it’s unclear that they will actually be able to start doing the work the government wants them to do.

“On top of that, the system is tightly bound by existing legislation. Local authorities [LAs] in particular have quite strict guidelines, and tribunals suggest that there are often disputes over eligibility for EHCPs but LAs are likely to be pulled towards the law as it stands until the law changes.”
output.standfirst: The government is investing in early intervention and specialist bases, but a thinktank says Labour’s Send overhaul could unravel before 2030, with councils projecting nearly one in 10 pupils will have an EHCP by 2029.
output.progress: The Department for Education says it is also widening access to specialists and training every teacher to support inclusion.

context.text: Georgia Gould visited a Colchester school last week that is already succeeding at mainstream Send inclusion, hoping to spread its best practice nationally.

output.headline: TaxWatch research shows billionaire's Monaco move long predates wealth tax plans
output.bodyHtml:
Research by TaxWatch has found that Reuben, 88, has been a tax resident in Monaco since at least 2014, years before reports suggested he had just quit the UK over a possible wealth tax.

A spokesperson for the Newcastle United shareholder, who with his brother Simon, 85, shares a combined estimated wealth of almost £28bn, confirmed this was the case.

The Sunday Times had reported that Reuben, one of the richest men in the UK, had apparently fled to the tax haven of Monaco after moving from his Holland Park house in London to live full-time in the principality, prompting much pearl-clutching.

Labour’s tax regime was blamed, with reports suggesting Reuben had probably left because of potential taxes on wealth in the upcoming budget, and fears of a cascading effect across the economy as wealth drained from the UK.

Related: Apparent exodus of super-rich suggests UK is no longer billionaires’ playground

Simon Reuben, 85, has lived in Monaco for 40 years since moving there on health grounds while having cancer.

The principality is popular with those who do not wish to pay UK taxes, as it imposes no income tax, capital gains tax or inheritance tax.

In July 2019, when David became a director of the Reuben foundation, paperwork filed at the UK company registry stated he was ‘usually resident’ in Monaco.

In 2024 he provided a signed declaration to a Los Angeles court stating: ‘I reside in Monaco. I have resided there for approximately 10 years.’

The Reuben brothers were reported to be ‘non-doms’, meaning they paid UK tax only on income generated in the UK. The then chancellor, Rachel Reeves, ended this system in April last year, prompting a reported exodus of foreign super-rich individuals.

Asked whether Reuben would have been caught by changes to these rules had he not already moved out of his UK residence, a spokesperson said: ‘That’s an entirely hypothetical question to which it would be impossible to give an answer.’

Mike Lewis, the director of TaxWatch, told the Guardian: ‘When we started looking into this, we were surprised that publicly available documents completely contradicted a major news story. Sadly, these kinds of stories dominate the UK’s public and political conversation about our tax system.

‘The autumn budget may see some of the biggest changes in years to how gains from wealth are taxed. Perhaps it’s time that our politicians, and our media, debate these changes based on public facts and verifiable numbers – not anecdotes and anonymous reports from billionaires and their spokespeople.’

The Labour MP Clive Lewis, who campaigns for a wealth tax, said: ‘If you want to live in this country, being British, having access to the culture of London, people want that, and there are lots of billionaires and millionaires who do stay because of that.

‘It’s instructive that there is a grouping of commentators who put on the scare tactics to say the wealthy are leaving this country. We can see that many of these billionaires don’t reside here anyway, many of them do stay here, and those who want to go, we can’t stop them anyway. This has always been the case.’

Some of the super-rich are leaving. Analysis of Bloomberg’s Billionaires Index has found that super-rich UK residents worth a combined £121bn have either left or loosened ties with the UK since the Labour government came to power in 2024 – more than half of all billionaire wealth.

Among those who have left are the steel magnate Lakshmi Mittal, the Aston Villa co-owner Nassef Sawiris and the shipping magnate John Fredriksen.

Inheritance tax changes in Reeves’s budget were also blamed for pushing the wealthy out, and capital gains tax is thought likely to rise this autumn.

The Reuben brothers were born in Mumbai, moved to London in their teens, and attended a state school in Islington, leaving education at 17 with no A-levels. They went on to build businesses in metal trading and carpet importing, and have since built a property empire.

They own prestigious locations including Mayfair’s chandelier-festooned Burlington Arcade, Admiralty Arch – now being developed into a five-star hotel – and Millbank Tower in Westminster.
output.standfirst: TaxWatch research finds David Reuben, 88, has been Monaco tax-resident since at least 2014, undercutting reports that he quit the UK over a possible wealth tax and sparked a wider billionaire exodus.
output.progress: TaxWatch has already corrected the public record, while Mike Lewis calls for debate based on facts, not anecdotes.

output.headline: Nearly half a million people choose wildlife for new UK banknotes
output.bodyHtml:
Barn owls, bumblebees, puffins and hedgehogs have been chosen by the public to feature on the next generation of Bank of England banknotes, after a consultation in which nearly half a million people took part – though the decision to retire historical figures such as Winston Churchill and Jane Austen prompted a backlash from opposition politicians.

Victoria Cleland, the Bank's chief cashier, said: "I am delighted that nearly half-a-million people responded to our wildlife imagery consultation, showing that cash still matters." She said the public had chosen "four distinct and inspiring animals" that not only showcased the great variety of wildlife in the UK but would "also enhance the security of our banknotes".

The quartet of creatures were selected after a large-scale consultation settled on wild animals as the theme, with members of the public then asked to pick their favourites out of 18 options divided into three categories.

The buff-tailed bumblebee got the most votes in the insects, fish and amphibian group; the barn owl won the bird division; and the European hedgehog was named top mammal. The Atlantic puffin was added to celebrate Britain's coastline, the Bank said.

It is as yet undecided which species will adorn which banknote. An image of King Charles will continue to be represented on the other side of the £5, £10, £20 and £50 notes, which are expected to take several years to design.

Among the species losing out were the basking shark, the common frog and the red fox – the latter celebrated in David Attenborough's recent Wild London documentary, but seen as a pest by some.

Atlantic puffins, with their distinctive multicoloured beaks, spend much of their lives at sea, coming ashore in summer to nest in burrows on islands off the coast including the Farne Islands and Lundy.

With their numbers declining, the bird is classified as "vulnerable" on the International Union for Conservation of Nature's red list of threatened species.

The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, accused the Bank of "erasing our history" after the decision to replace the historical figures on the banknotes – including Winston Churchill and Jane Austen – was first announced in March. Badenoch called it "a silly thing to do", adding: "I absolutely do not support it." Her Reform UK counterpart, Nigel Farage, described the move as "absolutely crackers".

The Liberal Democrat leader, Ed Davey, joined in, issuing a social media video in which he brandished a fiver and claimed that Churchill deserved "better than being replaced by a badger".

The badger was not among the 18-strong shortlist of animals eventually published by the Bank in June.

That selection prompted the RSPCA to complain about the choice of animals on offer, calling for less obviously cute creatures to be included. "Gulls, badgers, rats and pigeons all divide opinion, but this would have been a great opportunity to discuss these fantastic animals," it said.
output.standfirst: Barn owls, bumblebees, puffins and hedgehogs were voted onto Britain’s next banknotes, after dropping historical figures such as Churchill drew political criticism, while the RSPCA said the shortlist needed less obviously cute creatures.
output.progress: The Bank of England says the chosen designs will also strengthen banknote security as it finalises which creature appears on which note.

output.headline: Transplant breakthrough offers fertility hope to teenager after chemotherapy
output.bodyHtml:
Surgeons in the UK have carried out the country's first testicular tissue transplant on a teenager, offering hope that boys left infertile by chemotherapy could one day have biological children of their own.

The 19-year-old had his tissue removed and frozen three years ago before undergoing treatment for a serious blood disorder. He said he was “incredibly grateful” to the medical team behind the pioneering procedure, which represents a potential breakthrough for male fertility preservation.

Chemotherapy can permanently damage the cells needed to produce sperm, leaving children who undergo it at risk of infertility in adulthood. Three years after his chemotherapy, tests showed he had no sperm in his semen.

Now a team of NHS medics in Edinburgh have transplanted his previously frozen testicular tissue back into his body, in the hope that it will begin to produce sperm.

The operation is the first of its kind in the UK, and only the second reported to have taken place worldwide. “Fertility is something I’ve struggled with personally for a long time,” said the patient, who asked to remain anonymous.

“I’ve always wanted to have children of my own but at some point, I found myself starting to slowly accept that that might never be possible for me. Having this procedure has given me genuine hope for the future.”

The student added: “We don’t know yet whether it will work, but knowing that there is now even a possibility means more to me than I can really put into words.

“I’m incredibly grateful to everyone for giving me this opportunity and for all the work that has made it possible. I also hope that being part of this research means that, in the future, other young people in the same position can have that hope too.”

Freezing semen is an established fertility preservation method for older teenagers and adult men.

But for pre-pubescent boys this is not an option. The new treatment potentially opens a door to fertility preservation for children needing cancer care and other treatments which require the use of chemotherapy.

The tissue taken for transplant contains spermatogonial stem cells, which are responsible for producing sperm from puberty onwards.

Doctors should know in a matter of months whether the procedure, which took place in August, has enabled the 19-year-old to produce viable sperm.

The transplant, carried out by medics at NHS Lothian and backed by funding from Children with Cancer UK, follows a decade of research by the University of Edinburgh.

Rod Mitchell, professor of developmental endocrinology at Edinburgh’s Institute for Regeneration and Repair, and a consultant paediatric endocrinologist at NHS Lothian, said: “This is a big step towards helping boys facing treatments that damage their fertility to have children of their own.

“Ten years ago, we started our research programme to freeze and store pieces of testicle from boys before they start chemotherapy, to preserve their fertility.

Related: Cancer rates rising more quickly among younger people, international research finds

“We are beginning to see some of these young men return to explore their fertility options. This study offers real hope for future fertility in boys facing cancer treatment.”

Tracey Gillies, the medical director at NHS Lothian, said the operation was a “landmark procedure” and marked an important step forward for children whose fertility may be affected by treatment they needed to overcome serious illness.

She added: “We are grateful to the patient and his family for helping advance research that could transform care for others in the future.”

In May, the Guardian reported how a man whose testicular tissue was frozen before he had chemotherapy as a child and retransplanted 16 years later had been able to produce sperm.

More than 1,200 patients in the UK and 3,100 worldwide had had testicular tissue stored for potential future use, the University of Edinburgh said.
output.standfirst: In the UK's first operation of its kind, surgeons in Edinburgh transplanted a 19-year-old's own stored testicular tissue back into his body after chemotherapy for a serious blood disorder left him with no sperm.
output.progress: Doctors at NHS Lothian, whose transplant was funded by Children with Cancer UK, should know within months whether it has produced viable sperm.

output.headline: Russian health officials step up efforts to contain suspected plague outbreak
output.bodyHtml:
According to the Baikal Medical Journal, health officials in Irkutsk have taken extensive measures to stop a potential outbreak from spreading. Neighbours said workers in white protective suits and gas masks disinfected the two-storey brick building where Shipilova lived several times after her death last Friday.

“The smell was unbearable and very pungent,” a woman in her 40s said. “A woman knocked on our door. I said: ‘What are you treating here?’ I already knew about the plague rumours.

“She said: ‘It’s for cockroaches.’ But we don’t even have any cockroaches in our building. I saw her packing her overalls into a bag. I was like, ‘Well, I get it.’”

The World Health Organization has said it does not have the “full picture” from Russia following the suspected death from plague last week of a 28-year-old laboratory worker in Siberia.

At the same time, officials have imposed sweeping quarantine restrictions at the lab where Shipilova worked and in nearby hospitals. Staff were locked down inside the institute for three days, sleeping on the floors and on chairs, while tests were conducted.

Darya Shipilova died two days after falling ill with cold-like symptoms. She was an employee at the anti-plague research institute in the eastern city of Irkutsk, with some reports suggesting she was infected after a workplace accident.

The Russian authorities have denied a connection with the institute and say Shipilova died from “pneumonia of an unknown aetiology”. They insist there is no danger of a plague outbreak and have described the “sanitary and epidemiological” situation in the region as stable.

Related: What do we know about death of anti-plague institute worker in Russia and is there a wider risk?

On Wednesday the WHO director general, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said: “We don’t yet have the full picture of this event and we’re not able to conduct a full risk assessment.

“Timely, complete and transparent information sharing is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public risks.”

Tedros said he also wanted more clarification from the Russian government following unconfirmed media reports of “a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause”.

“We assess any reporting from the community,” he said. “We asked Russia to respond to that. We’re waiting for an answer.”

The WHO’s director of epidemic and pandemic management, Maria Van Kerkhove, said the agency still did not know how Shipilova became infected in the first place – and with what viral disease. If pneumonic plague was ruled out, “what did she actually die from?” Kerkhove asked.

In an interview with local media, Shipilova’s 64-year-old mother, Svetlana, discounted the theory that her daughter had been infected after smashing a test tube. “I know the truth. I’m fending off stupid friends who believe this. A test tube is unbreakable, even if you throw it against the wall,” she said.

She described her daughter as a dedicated worker and “pure person” devoted to her job.

Former classmates are also sceptical she was infected at her workplace. One reportedly said: “They’ve smeared a woman without properly investigating. Knowing how hard-working and responsible she was, it just doesn’t add up for me.”

The Kremlin has sought to downplay the incident and has brushed aside an offer of assistance made earlier this week by Donald Trump, the US president. The White House has pressed Moscow for more details of the case, while stressing the risk to the US is very low.

On Tuesday Trump said he would speak about the plague issue “very soon” with Vladimir Putin, who celebrated his 74th birthday on Wednesday. The Kremlin said no call had been arranged but could be quickly organised.
output.standfirst: Russian officials quarantined and tested lab staff after the suspected death from plague of a Siberian worker, but the WHO says it still lacks a ‘full picture’ and needs transparent information from Moscow.
output.progress: Health officials in Irkutsk have quarantined and tested institute staff and repeatedly disinfected buildings to contain any potential outbreak.

output.headline: Blind patients regain partial sight in trial of Nobel-winning gene therapy
output.bodyHtml:
A gene therapy based on Nobel prize-winning science has been shown to be safe and can partly restore sight in blind people, researchers have revealed.

The approach, known as optogenetic therapy, harnesses the technique for turning nerve cells on and off using light that scooped the 2026 Nobel prize in physiology or medicine.

It was first shown to partly restore vision in a single blind person in 2021. Now researchers have reported the results from a larger trial involving the original patient and a further nine people.

“What we can say for sure is that the concept of optogenetics is valid for vision restoration,” said Prof Botond Roska, director of the Institute of Molecular and Clinical Ophthalmology Basel and a lead author of the study.

Roska added the aim is now to work towards restoring high-resolution vision, with the hope of achieving the goal in five to 10 years.

All 10 of the trial participants had advanced retinitis pigmentosa – a group of genetic disorders thought to affect more than 1.5 million people worldwide.

In these disorders, light-sensitive cells in the retina gradually lose their function. However, ganglion cells in the retina, which send visual information to the brain, deteriorate less quickly.

“These cells are not the primary cells targeted by the disease, so that’s why they are good candidates for the therapy,” said Dr José-Alain Sahel, another lead author of the study from the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center in the US.

The gene therapy involves giving a single injection into the eye. This injection contains a harmless, synthetic virus that delivers the genetic instructions for producing a light-sensitive protein into a ring of surviving ganglion cells. As a result, these cells are made light-sensitive.

Each patient then receives a pair of light-stimulating goggles. These capture images of the world around the patient and convert them into pulses of light of a single wavelength. These pulses activate the ganglion cells that have been made light-sensitive, allowing the wearer to perceive a monochrome image.

Crucially, the technique does not depend on the exact genetic cause of the patient’s sight loss.

Writing in the New England Journal of Medicine, the researchers report how for each patient they treated only the eye with the worst vision, adding participants’ outcomes were then followed for up to five years.

Only one severe eye-related side-effect occurred, but this was resolved within minutes, and there were no side effects related to the therapy in the rest of the body.

Six of the 10 participants had clinically meaningful improvements in light sensitivity after the treatment.

What’s more, some of the participants showed improvements in a range of tasks when wearing the light-stimulating goggles after the gene therapy – such as detecting, locating and touching a notebook, locating a door and walking on a line.

The team added that participants who spent more time training with the goggles tended to do better on the tasks.

The study does have limitations: “[Patients] can detect objects, but they cannot yet detect faces,” said Roska. That, the team say, is down to the treated ganglion cells being in a ring-like arrangement around the fovea – the tiny pit in the retina responsible for sharp central vision.

Mark Hankins, professor of visual neuroscience at the University of Oxford, who was not involved in the work, welcomed the study, noting it provides reassurance on the safety of the approach and its application to people who still have some residual vision.

“We’ve gone from one patient to 10 patients, we’ve seen improvement in their light sensitivity … and we’ve seen that we can give a stable restoration of some visual function, some light sensitivity, that lasts for four or five years in these patients,” he said. “They’re baby steps, but they’re critical.”
output.standfirst: A gene therapy built on Nobel prize-winning optogenetics let six of 10 blind trial patients partly regain light sensitivity, though they could not yet detect faces, researchers say.
output.progress: Researchers are now working to restore high-resolution vision, aiming to achieve that goal within five to 10 years.

output.headline: Software written by Margaret Hamilton saved Apollo 11’s moon landing
output.bodyHtml:
Margaret Hamilton, the software pioneer whose code powered the first moon landing, has died, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) announced on Wednesday. She was 90.

At a time before titles such as software engineer and computer scientist had become mainstream, Hamilton, who died on 30 September, learned to program under the tutelage of a renowned MIT meteorologist.

She went on to sharpen that craft in an MIT laboratory, writing software that could detect enemy aircraft, and when the institute won a Nasa contract to develop the Apollo onboard flight software, she seized the opportunity.

Related: Margaret Hamilton: ‘They worried that the men might rebel. They didn’t’

“I was attracted both by the sheer idea and the fact that it had never been done before. I was the first programmer to join and the first woman they hired,” she told the Guardian in 2019.

In 1969, minutes before the Apollo 11 spacecraft was due to make history by landing on the lunar surface, an alarm rang on its onboard computer, signalling an emergency.

Facing a decision on whether to abort, the spacecraft continued on: the software was working exactly as Hamilton and her team had intended.

“It quickly became clear the software was not only informing everyone that there was a hardware-related problem but was compensating for it – restarting and re-establishing the highest priority tasks. The error detection and recovery mechanisms had come to the rescue,” Hamilton said.

Barack Obama recalled the episode in 2016, when he presented her with the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

“Our astronauts didn’t have much time, but thankfully they had Margaret Hamilton,” he said.

Hamilton is survived by her daughter, a son-in-law, two grandsons and four great grandchildren, according to MIT.

Looking back on the mission, in a 2009 interview with MIT News, Hamilton said: “Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers; no time to be beginners.”
output.standfirst: Her software compensated for a hardware-related problem revealed by an alarm indicating an emergency during the 1969 landing, an achievement that later earned her the Presidential Medal of Freedom; Margaret Hamilton has died aged 90.

output.headline: Education secretary meets Ethan Scott Brown's family amid Crown Office investigation
output.bodyHtml:
The family of a student who took his own life after being wrongly told he would not be eligible to graduate have said the University of Glasgow “will be held to account”.

Ethan Scott Brown, 23, was due to graduate in December 2024 after studying geography.

However, his family said that in September that year, the university told him he had not been awarded a grade for one course and would therefore not be eligible to graduate with an honours degree.

His family said as a result, he took his own life on 13 December 2024, the day he should have been graduating.

He was found dead in his bedroom by his mother, Tracy Scott, that morning.

Scott, who collected her son’s degree posthumously, has called for a fatal accident inquiry to be held into his death.

The university has said it is “profoundly sorry” and is implementing a series of recommendations after a review.

The university’s internal inquiry found “systemic” errors in the way Brown’s degree had been graded, and that he had enough marks for a 2:1 honours degree. It also found that although Brown had told staff that he had concerns about his mental health, they had failed to offer him support.

On Tuesday it was reported that the family had settled a civil court action with the university. The sum of the settlement has not been disclosed.

On Wednesday, the family met the Scottish education secretary, Màiri McAllan, at St Andrew’s House in Edinburgh.

Speaking after the meeting, their solicitor Aamer Anwar said they had placed “the University of Glasgow on notice that they will be held to account”.

Anwar claimed that in its drive to become a global institution, the university had “forgotten its soul”.

He added: “Their failures were catastrophic and systemic. They failed not just in their duty of care to Ethan, but to many other students over the years.

“Today’s meeting with the minister was important and was welcomed. The minister offered to ask the QAA [Quality Assurance Agency for Higher Education], who are investigating the university, to meet with the family.

“The family welcomed the apology by Ms McAllan for her predecessor’s statement in September 2025 which implied an acceptance of the university’s position that Ethan’s case was an isolated incident.”

Anwar added that the university’s governance process was “not fit for purpose”.

A spokesperson for the University of Glasgow said: “The university is profoundly sorry that Ethan tragically took his own life and fully understands the deep distress this has caused his family. We repeat our sincere apology as well as our deepest sympathy.

“Following an internal investigation into assessment regulations, the university self-referred to the Scottish Funding Council.

“The Quality Assurance Agency subsequently carried out a targeted peer review, which resulted in a series of recommendations for action.

“The university fully accepted the recommendations and is on track to implement them.”

A spokesperson for the Crown Office said the circumstances of Brown’s death were being investigated by the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service, adding that the family would be kept updated on any developments.

  • In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123, or email jo@samaritans.org or jo@samaritans.ie. In the US, you can call or text the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline on 988, chat on 988lifeline.org, or text HOME to 741741 to connect with a crisis counselor. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org
output.standfirst: Ethan Scott Brown’s family have met the education secretary; the Crown Office is investigating his death after the 23-year-old took his own life when the University of Glasgow wrongly told him he could not graduate.
output.progress: The Crown Office is investigating the death, and the family’s solicitor says the university will be held to account.

output.headline: Elm that resisted Dutch elm disease named UK's tree of the year
output.bodyHtml:
The “astonishing and bizarre” Bendy Tree in Northern Ireland has triumphed in this year’s tree of the year competition, taking the title of overall winner.

Related: Half a million trees to be planted in England in three years, says government

The wych elm tree, located in Newcastle, County Down, owes its name to its near horizontal trunk, which has grown sideways owing to the strong seaside winds coming off the Irish Sea.

The 150-year-old tree has resisted Dutch elm disease, a fungus that has destroyed most of the UK’s 30m elms, making it a worthy winner of the competition’s “against the odds” theme.

The tree was originally planted in the mid-19th century as part of a row of wych elms along the town’s promenade to shelter the main street from sea winds, and has outlasted its neighbours: many of those trees were felled during redevelopments of the town, leaving the bendy tree the last one standing.

“When you look at this astonishing and bizarre tree, there’s no doubt about what it has endured,” said May Chemais, ancient tree inventory lead for the Woodland Trust, the charity that runs the annual competition.

“We’ve all been through changes and hardships that have shaped who we are: I think that’s why the Bendy Tree has struck a chord with people,” she said.

For John Martin, director of the Woodland Trust NI, it is the whimsical nature of the tree that makes it a worthy winner.

Related: Could you be an ‘autumn spotter’? Public asked to track changing colours of trees in England

Having grown up visiting Newcastle as a child, Martin recalls seeing the tree out of the corner of his eye and being surprised to see a tree growing this way.

“You expect nature to behave in a certain way and we would expect a tree, most of the time, to grow upwards, whereas this one has grown sideways,” he said. “I guess it gives people a bit of a smile on their day.”

The tree’s unusual shape has also provided welcome shade to residents and visitors resting on the bench located beneath its branches.

“Older trees like this one are providing our communities with so much – from shade, wellbeing and health benefits, to stories, culture and pride of place,” said Chemais.

Other trees nominated in this year’s competition included the Crowhurst Yew in Crowhurst, Surrey, England. Villagers hollowed out the trunk in 1820 to create a parish meeting room within the tree.
